chunks: Faḍālah ibn Sīnān, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) who said:

A man from Banī Fahd passed by the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) while he was beating his slave, and the slave was saying, 'I seek refuge with Allah,' yet the man did not desist from him. When the slave saw the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), he said, 'I seek refuge with Muḥammad,' so the man stopped beating him. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'He seeks refuge with Allah, yet you do not grant him protection; he seeks refuge with Muḥammad, so you grant him protection? By Allah, His one who seeks refuge is more deserving of protection than [one who seeks refuge with] Muḥammad.' The man said, 'He is free for the sake of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'By the One who sent me as a Prophet with truth, if you had not done so, your face would have fallen into the heat of the Fire.'
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the slave seeking refuge in Allah versus Prophet Muhammad in this hadith?
ai.summary: This incident, recorded in *Kitab al-Zuhd*, illustrates the practical authority of the Prophet’s name as a source of sanctuary (*jiwar*) in early Islamic society, where invoking his name carried immediate social weight. The master’s prompt release of the slave upon hearing 'Muhammad' underscores the high status of the Ahl al-Bayt and the Prophet, while the warning of 'face touching Hell' emphasizes the spiritual consequence of neglecting this divine right. This narrative serves as a foundational text for understanding the intercession and protective power attributed to the Prophet in Shia tradition.
